definition: Hierarchical means organized into ranked levels in which each tier holds more authority than the one below it.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word hierarchical. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know hierarchical should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The monastery was strictly hierarchical, and no novice dared speak before the elder monks had each said their piece in order of seniority.
A flat organization has no levels of authority at all — everyone is a peer — whereas a hierarchical one builds a working ladder of command.
A loosely ranked group has some sense of who is senior but rarely enforces it; a hierarchical group gives each tier real authority over the one below.

Ranked simply means placed in a definite order of standing, with some members above others — the plainest word for the idea. Hierarchical says more: the order is built into a system of levels, and each level holds real authority over the one below.

Tiered stresses the picture of distinct levels stacked like layers, whether or not the levels command each other — tiered seating and tiered pricing rank nothing. Hierarchical adds power to the picture: each tier in a hierarchical system outranks and directs the one beneath it.

Stratified is the formal, often academic word for a system settled into fixed layers or classes, and it emphasizes how sealed-off and permanent the layers themselves are. Hierarchical focuses instead on the working chain of authority that runs from each level down to the next.
Describes a system in which everyone holds equal standing and equal say, with no ranked tiers of authority — the direct opposite of a hierarchical arrangement.
Describes a group run by equals who share authority and make decisions together as colleagues, rather than one arranged into ranks that command each other.
No wedding date in the family was ever announced until the matriarch had approved it.
Hierarchical means organized into ranked levels in which each tier holds more authority than the one below it.
In the royal court, hierarchical rules of precedence dictated that a baron must yield to a duke, a duke to the crown prince, and everyone alike to the reigning monarch.

Notice why "hierarchical" is exact here: the court is not merely tidy or well-run, it is arranged into ranked levels of authority, where each tier can command the one beneath it and must defer to the one above.
A looser word like "organized" would only tell you the court had some structure or order, it would not tell you that a duke actually outranks a baron and can overrule him.
Hierarchical always carries that extra idea of tiers of power stacked one above another, not just parts arranged neatly side by side.
"hierarchical" is a precise, slightly formal word at home in essays, workplace descriptions, and academic writing.
In casual speech people often just say a group is "top-down" or has "a pecking order," but "hierarchical" is the word to reach for when you want to sound exact and analytical.

Medicine there is unapologetically hierarchical.
